nutshell: Inflation concerns resurface, driven by Middle East geopolitical risks and a surge in oil prices.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: This is the March 4th closing bell briefing. It was a tough day on Wall Street, with all three major indices finishing lower.

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: That's right. Today's market can be summed up by rising inflation fears fueled by geopolitical risk in the Middle East and a spike in oil prices. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.83%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.94%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 1.02%. Notably, West Texas Intermediate crude oil surged over 4% in a single day to top $74 a barrel, and the 10-year Treasury yield also climbed, weighing on the broader market.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: With oil prices jumping that much, it seems the geopolitical risk in the Middle East was clearly the main driver.

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Exactly. News broke that maritime transport through the Strait of Hormuz, which handles about 20% of the world's oil, has come to a virtual standstill as military conflict with Iran intensifies. This sparked major concerns about the oil supply chain, causing prices to surge and immediately feeding into inflation pressures. Investors reacted by reducing their exposure to risk assets, worried about the impact of higher energy costs on corporate expenses and consumer prices.

sources.title: Oil prices soar again and stocks crumble as Iran war escalates

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: And how did the economic data released today play into this situation?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: It was really a case of bad news piling on. The ISM Services PMI released today came in stronger than expected, showing the services sector remains robust. Normally, that would be positive news, but with inflation alarms already ringing due to the oil spike, it was interpreted as giving the Fed more reason to keep interest rates higher for longer. So, the combination of a strong economy and an oil shock reinforced the 'higher-for-longer' narrative, deepening the market's decline.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: I see. So it was a double whammy for the market: the oil price surge and the fear of higher-for-longer rates.

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Yes, that's right. And the market is particularly concerned because this oil price spike seems different from past incidents.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: Different from the past? Could you elaborate on that, starting with the situation in the Middle East?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Right, this oil shock stems from an actual supply chain disruption, not just geopolitical tension. Iran's Revolutionary Guard declared the closure of the Strait of Hormuz—which, again, handles about 20% of global oil transport—and even released footage of a tanker being hit, effectively halting maritime traffic. On that news, WTI crude skyrocketed over 9% intraday, threatening the $76 a barrel mark, while Brent crude neared $83. This sent an immediate shockwave through the stock market, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq falling around 1% each. Unusually, even safe-haven assets like Treasuries saw a sell-off, pushing the 10-year yield higher. This shows the market isn't just in a simple risk-off mode; it's starting to price in both the inflationary pressure from the oil surge and the resulting possibility of the Fed staying hawkish for longer.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: So, just as oil-driven inflation fears were mounting, we got a signal that the economy is strong. Why did good economic data end up hurting the market?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: It was a classic case of 'good news is bad news.' The March ISM Services PMI came in above expectations, confirming that the services sector, which makes up over two-thirds of the U.S. economy, is still expanding strongly. In normal times, this would be great news, easing recession fears. But it's a different story when inflation anxieties are at a peak due to surging oil. The market interpreted this data as giving the Fed justification to maintain higher rates for longer and more aggressively to combat inflation. Ultimately, with inflationary pressure confirmed from both the supply side (oil) and the demand side (a strong economy), rate cut expectations retreated even further, putting significant pressure on growth stocks, especially in the tech sector.

sources.title: Iran attacks threaten US economy with more uncertainty around inflation, growth
Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq plunge, oil surges as fresh strikes intensify Iran conflict

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: So, it seems both factors—supply chain instability and a strong economy—are pointing to the same conclusion: higher rates for longer. What will the market be watching for next?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Yes, all eyes are now on the Fed's next move. Investors will be looking for clues in the Fed's Beige Book, set to be released today, to see how the regional Feds are assessing recent inflation pressures and economic conditions. Also, the March non-farm payrolls report later this week will be the most critical piece of data to either confirm or contradict the economic strength shown in today's ISM report. With some investment banks like JPMorgan warning that this Middle East situation could be a prolonged issue, unlike past short-term shocks, the market is likely to remain volatile for a while, caught between geopolitical news and macroeconomic data as it tries to gauge the path of inflation and Fed policy.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: Right, and speaking of that volatility, one of the stocks with the most dramatic moves today, tied to the geopolitical risk, was Lockheed Martin. It looked like it was about to hit a new all-time high at the open, but then it reversed sharply and closed down more than 2%.

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Yes, that was a classic 'blow-off top' pattern, a signal of a short-term peak. The news of escalating conflict with Iran certainly pushed investor sentiment on defense stocks into extreme greed, which drove the stock to an all-time high right after the opening bell. But the powerful sell-off that followed shows the other side of the story. Separate from the crowd psychology reacting to headlines, it appears some investors took profits based on fundamental risk factors disclosed in the company's recent annual report. Today's price action can be seen as the result of a clash between these two perspectives.

sources.title: The market winners: Which stocks are 'boosted' by the Iran war so far?

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: When you say risk factors from the annual report, what specifically are you referring to?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: The biggest concern is the collapse in profitability of its core Aeronautics division, which accounts for about 40% of the company's total revenue. According to the 2025 annual report, this division's operating margin plummeted from 8.8% a year ago to a dismal 6.9%. This was due to a massive $950 million loss on a specific classified fixed-price contract. What's more serious is that this isn't a one-off event but part of a worsening pattern. The company itself warned in its filing about the potential for additional significant losses in the future, which raises questions about its fundamental cash-generating ability.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: A decline in profitability in a core division is definitely a serious issue. But isn't there also a positive view that new growth drivers like hypersonic missiles or the space business could offset these problems?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: That's a very important point, and it's true that the Missiles and Fire Control (MFC) division posted 14% revenue growth. However, this could be a 'sweet poison' that masks the structural problems in the Aeronautics division. Because the Aeronautics business is so large, the collapse in its profit margins creates a hole that's difficult to fill with growth from other divisions alone. The more fundamental issue is that this fixed-price contract risk isn't unique to Aeronautics. The MFC division has a history of similar multi-billion dollar losses, which suggests this is a company-wide, structural risk embedded in the business model itself, not just a mistake by one department.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: I see. So that means the massive backlog, worth about $193.6 billion, can't be viewed as purely positive either.

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Exactly. A backlog can be a strong moat ensuring future stability, but it can also be a ticking time bomb filled with unprofitable contracts. The recurring large-scale losses suggest Lockheed Martin has a fundamental difficulty in forecasting and controlling costs on complex development programs. In this context, the sheer size of the backlog can create an optical illusion, masking the qualitative risks within. It seems the market today got excited by the short-term geopolitical news, but then quickly cooled off as it realized the weight of the structural risks detailed in the financial statements. This appears to be a time when risk management is key.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: Could you summarize today's market in one sentence, and then point out the key economic events we should be watching?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Overall, today was a day for the market to catch its breath. The major indices finished mixed, digesting the recent rally. Now, all eyes are turning to the employment-related data concentrated at the end of this week. It's no exaggeration to call this 'Jobs Data Week,' as these will be the final key data points for gauging the timing of the Fed's rate cuts.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: You mentioned 'Jobs Data Week'—which specific indicators should we be keeping an eye on?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: Yes, first, tomorrow's Challenger Job Cuts report will give us a glimpse into corporate layoff trends. But the main event is the February jobs report, due out Friday morning local time. The market expects non-farm payrolls to have slowed significantly to 60,000 new jobs, down from the previous figure of 130,000. The unemployment rate is expected to hold steady at 4.3%, and average hourly earnings, which show wage growth, are forecast to rise 0.3% month-over-month, a slight slowdown from the prior reading.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: So, how might the market react depending on the outcome of this jobs report?

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: The market is walking a very fine line right now. If the jobs number comes in too strong, it could push back expectations for a Fed rate cut, which would weigh on the market. On the other hand, if it's too weak, it could spark concerns about a recession. What the market is really hoping for is a 'Goldilocks' number—not too hot, not too cold. Essentially, it wants to see a signal that the labor market is cooling but not collapsing. Therefore, it's worth keeping in mind that we could see increased volatility right after the report is released.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: Right, it's shaping up to be a crucial week for gauging the market's direction ahead of the Fed's decision. A cautious approach seems warranted for investors.

scripts.speaker: 해설자
scripts.text: That's right. It's a time to focus on reading the broader macroeconomic trend rather than getting swayed by short-term volatility. This jobs report will be a key turning point in assessing that trend.

scripts.speaker: 진행자
scripts.text: Thank you for your insights today. That concludes our March 4th closing bell briefing.
